<reason>Side B (PRO) built the stronger path to victory by establishing concrete, pharmacologically grounded mechanisms by which punitive enforcement increases overdose deaths—specifically the lethal tolerance loss following brief jail stints and the isolation that suppresses 911 calls—and by linking criminal records directly to economic desperation and downstream crime. The decisive moment came when Side B's Pressure Question Q1 exposed a fatal contradiction in Side A's case: CON required a "coercive backstop" to compel treatment, yet in Rebuttal 2 defined that backstop as clinical tools (medical detention, residential treatment, health commissions) rather than criminal jail. Side B's closing effectively framed this as a concession proving that decriminalization can retain clinical leverage while eliminating the lethal criminal machinery. While Side A raised a valid concern about loss of leverage, they failed to demonstrate why civil commitment and administrative sanctions—available without criminalization—could not serve the same function, leaving their core causal claim vulnerable.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side B's Pressure Question Q1 ("When an addict relapses during mandated treatment, what is that 'coercive backstop' in practice, if not the exact jail stint that destroys tolerance...") and the subsequent Rebuttal 2 answer A1, which exposed that CON had redefined their backstop as clinical interventions (medical detention) available under decriminalization, thereby collapsing the distinction between CON's preferred "coerced treatment" and PRO's public health model.</best_rebuttal>
